title: Scaling Agentic AI Globally: Tencent Connects Experience, Engineering, And Ecosystem
summary: Tencent is connecting experience, engineering, and ecosystem as it seeks to scale agentic AI from enterprise production in China to global markets.
body_markdown:
At last year’s Tencent Cloud International Summit, we[described](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/a-tale-of-two-engines-meet-the-new-tencent/) Tencent’s strategy as a tale of two engines: AI as the intelligent engine and globalization as the expansion engine. A year later, those engines remain important, but they are becoming more closely connected. Agentic AI is moving from models and experiments into the everyday environments where people work, enterprises operate, and digital ecosystems interact. At the same time, Tencent wants to bring the technology, products, and operational experience developed in China to customers around the world.


At the sixth Tencent Cloud Global Industry Analyst Conference and the 2026 Tencent Global Digital Ecosystem Summit in Shenzhen, Tencent showed how it intends to support that transition. The company is moving beyond model development toward connecting models, agents, enterprise data, infrastructure, security, applications, and partners into a broader production system that can support both domestic transformation and international expansion.


Three themes stood out to us: **experience, engineering, and ecosystem** . Experience determines whether AI becomes embedded in the flow of everyday work. Engineering determines whether agents can operate reliably, securely, and economically at scale. And ecosystem determines whether Tencent can connect its technology and operational know-how with customers and partners across industries and markets.


## **Experience: From AI Assistants To AI-Native Work**


AI adoption is shifting from asking a chatbot questions toward giving agents goals, context, tools, and permission to act. This changes the user experience. Instead of switching among AI assistants, applications, documents, and enterprise systems, employees increasingly expect AI to follow their work across these boundaries. Tencent is using its extensive collaboration and application portfolio to make this experience increasingly continuous, contextual, and action-oriented. Major moves include:


- **Buddy One aims to connect AI around work rather than individual applications.** Tencent launched Buddy One as an integrated suite centered on WorkBuddy, designed to connect Tencent Docs, ima, Tencent Design, meetings, storage, and other tools through shared identity, data, and AI entitlements. WorkBuddy is intended to retrieve authorized information across applications and invoke different tools according to the task while allowing teams to continue editing and validating the results. The important shift is toward moving beyond copilots embedded in individual applications toward organizing applications around an AI-mediated task. For enterprises, this makes the battle for AI productivity increasingly about controlling the working context surrounding the model, not simply providing access to the best model.
- **Memory and context become part of the employee experience.** Tencent positioned its newly launched Tencent Netdisk as a unified memory space for the agent era, preserving context and AI-generated outputs so WorkBuddy can reuse them later. Tencent is also deepening WorkBuddy’s integration with WeCom, allowing authorized conversations, documents, and meeting records to become usable enterprise context. Through MCP interfaces, agents can connect with business applications such as ERP and CRM systems. This points toward an important evolution in enterprise AI: User experience will increasingly depend on how well agents maintain context across time and systems while respecting identity, permissions, and data boundaries.
- **Models are being optimized around real work, not just benchmarks.** Tencent announced that its next Hunyuan flagship model, Hy4, and the lighter Hy4 Flash are coming soon. Hy4 will strengthen long-horizon tasks and reasoning efficiency and add visual understanding, while Hy4 Flash targets higher-frequency, cost-sensitive workloads while retaining visual and agent capabilities. Tencent is also emphasizing closer co-design between models and applications. This reflects where enterprise model competition is heading: Model intelligence remains important, but enterprises will increasingly care about task completion, latency, reliability, multimodality, and cost within actual agent workflows.


## **Engineering: Agentic AI Forces The Cloud Stack To Evolve**


Better experiences alone will not put agents into production. Unlike traditional applications that execute relatively predictable transactions, agents can maintain state, reason across multiple steps, access changing context, invoke external tools, and remain active for extended periods. That pushes cloud architecture beyond conventional application hosting and model serving toward a new[context and harness engineering stack](https://www.forrester.com/report/the-technology-leaders-primer-for-context-engineering-and-contextops/RES202779) for agent execution. Tencent’s announcements reflected this shift across AI infrastructure, models, agent runtimes, security, and cloud operations. Major moves include:


- **Agent Runtime is emerging as a distinct infrastructure layer.** Tencent described an Agent Runtime designed for stateful and long-running agent workloads, with capabilities such as session isolation, pause-and-resume execution, snapshot-based startup, pooled networking, tiered data loading, MicroVM isolation, and request-level authorization. Tencent also announced further Agent Runtime upgrades and support for heterogeneous computing environments. The architectural implication extends beyond Tencent: As agent workloads scale, enterprises will need a runtime layer that manages identity, state, context, tools, execution, observability, isolation, and resource consumption across the agent lifecycle, much as cloud-native architecture established specialized runtime patterns for containerized applications.
- **AI infrastructure is becoming heterogeneous and token-centric.** Tencent highlighted its own servers and networking hardware alongside its Galaxy 128-GPU supernode and compatibility with mainstream accelerators. It is also opening TokenHub for access to models including Hunyuan, DeepSeek, GLM, MiniMax, and Kimi, while providing unified model access and billing. This matters because production AI increasingly becomes an infrastructure optimization problem across models, accelerators, inference engines, and workload patterns. Enterprises should evaluate whether their AI platform can route workloads across these resources while retaining visibility into performance, availability, and token economics rather than optimizing each component independently.
- **Trust must become an engineering property of the agent stack.** Tencent described its “Trusted AI” approach around controlling agent behavior, tracing execution, and governing data, with protections spanning malicious instruction detection, high-risk action blocking, identity and access management, execution tracing, encryption, and recovery. The summit also devoted product tracks to agent security, infrastructure, AIOps, AI-native databases, and enterprise knowledge. Enterprises should treat these capabilities as architectural requirements rather than security add-ons. The more authority an agent receives to retrieve information and execute actions, the more governance must operate at runtime, where organizations can continuously enforce identity, permissions, isolation, guardrails, observability, and human intervention.
- **AI is also becoming part of cloud operations itself.** Tencent’s MigraQ platform applies AI across resource discovery, product mapping, architecture design, cost assessment, migration planning, implementation, and rollback. At the analyst summit, Tencent highlighted a Southeast Asian telecom migration involving 1,200 microservices, 1,100 APIs, and more than 15 TB of data. This illustrates a broader opportunity beyond building AI applications: Cloud providers can productize their operational knowledge as agents that help customers design, migrate, operate, and troubleshoot increasingly complex environments. Eventually, the differentiation of an[AI-native cloud](https://www.forrester.com/report/embrace-the-ai-native-cloud-now/RES183626) may depend as much on how intelligently it operates infrastructure as on how efficiently it hosts AI.


## **Ecosystem: Tencent Wants AI To Learn From And Extend Its Digital Network**


Tencent’s biggest differentiator may ultimately lie outside the model itself. Its consumer services, collaboration products, enterprise applications, developer community, industry customers, and partners create multiple surfaces through which agents can obtain context, execute tasks, and reach users. This year’s Digital Ecosystem Summit reflects that ambition, with more than 100 AI products and new capabilities, hundreds of agent practices, dozens of thematic sessions, and dedicated tracks for different professional personas. The opportunity now is to turn those assets into an open and repeatable AI ecosystem.


- **Tencent is opening the agent platform beyond its own applications.** WorkBuddy supports enterprise-built and third-party agents as well as third-party messaging systems, while Tencent Cloud ADP enables companies to build customized business agents for workflows such as customer service, marketing, and operations. Tencent says WorkBuddy Enterprise has expanded into more than 50 industries since launching in March, while its open platform has attracted more than 50,000 partners and developers and accumulated more than 200,000 Skills. The strategic test will be whether Tencent can turn this breadth into a genuinely interoperable agent ecosystem in which models, agents, skills, tools, identities, and context remain portable enough for enterprises to avoid a new generation of AI silos.
- **Industry knowledge can become a flywheel for agent improvement.** Tencent centered the Digital Ecosystem Summit on a “multi-agent and data-driven flywheel” and is showcasing hundreds of agent practices across industries and business functions. Rather than treating these simply as references, Tencent can convert implementation patterns, operational lessons, and reusable skills into platform assets that shorten subsequent deployments. This is potentially where ecosystem becomes an engineering advantage. Cloud providers that systematically turn customer and partner experience into reusable agent patterns, connectors, skills, evaluation methods, and governance controls can reduce the gap between an impressive agent prototype and a repeatable production implementation.
- **Tencent is taking its agentic AI ecosystem global, not merely expanding cloud capacity.** Tencent Cloud says its overseas active customer base has doubled and its business now reaches more than 150 countries and regions. Its global ambition increasingly centers on bringing together infrastructure, data, agents, industry solutions, and operational expertise rather than simply adding overseas cloud regions. To succeed, Tencent must adapt the products and practices developed in China to different languages, regulations, application environments, partner networks, and customer expectations. Enterprises should assess its capabilities market by market, particularly around data residency, model availability, regulatory alignment, interoperability, local support, and integration with the technology ecosystems already used in each region.


## **What Enterprise Leaders Should Do Next**


Tencent’s announcements demonstrate how quickly agentic AI is expanding beyond models into employee experiences, infrastructure, data, security, and digital ecosystems. Tencent’s strategic opportunity is to turn its application footprint, engineering capacity, and broad ecosystem into a coherent agentic environment in which the model becomes one component of a larger system for understanding context, coordinating tools, and completing work. They also provide another reason for global enterprises to revisit established perceptions of Chinese technology vendors as their capabilities and international ambitions evolve. Technology leaders should take an outcome-driven approach to reassess vendor capabilities in each regional market, considering where they can deliver the right combination of business value, technical capabilities, ecosystem fit, governance, and local support. Against this backdrop, enterprises should consider how experience, engineering, and ecosystem need to evolve together as they scale agentic AI. To begin:


- **Design agentic AI around experiences, not standalone assistants.** The next wave of enterprise AI will be defined less by individual copilots and more by how agents work across applications, data, content, and business processes. Enterprises should start with high-value employee and customer journeys, then determine what models, context, tools, and agents are needed to support them. This shifts the focus from deploying AI features toward redesigning how work gets done.
- **Engineer for agents as a new class of workload.** Long-running sessions, dynamic context, tool use, autonomous actions, and variable inference require new approaches to runtime, identity, observability, security, and cost management. Enterprises should treat trusted execution and guardrails as architectural requirements while maintaining flexibility across models, infrastructure, and agent frameworks. The goal is to build an agentic AI foundation that can scale without sacrificing control, economics, or architectural choice.
- **Build an open ecosystem that can scale globally.** Agentic AI increasingly depends on interconnected applications, data, APIs, agents, skills, developers, and partners. Enterprises should establish interoperability and governance standards that allow agents to operate across this ecosystem while recognizing that AI doesn’t travel unchanged across markets. Global deployments must accommodate local languages, regulations, data residency, technology environments, and business practices while preserving common architecture and governance wherever possible.
